intro: Use comparative adjectives to compare two things and superlative adjectives to identify the highest or lowest degree in a group of three or more. Build the form that matches the adjective and the sentence.

sections.title: Short adjectives: -er and -est
sections.text: Most short adjectives take -er for a comparison and -est for a superlative: tall → taller → tallest. If the adjective ends in -e, add -r or -st: large → larger → largest. For a short consonant-vowel-consonant word, double the final consonant: big → bigger → biggest.
examples: This box is bigger than that tray.
This is the largest poster in the hall.
sections.note: Do not double after two consonants or after w, x or y.

sections.title: Adjectives ending in -y
sections.text: Many common two-syllable adjectives ending in consonant + y change y to i before -er and -est: easy → easier → easiest; busy → busier → busiest. This is not every final-y word: shy → shyer → shyest is a standard exception.
examples: This clue is easier than the final clue.
It is the noisiest part of the task.

sections.title: Longer adjectives and valid alternatives
sections.text: Longer adjectives usually use more and most: more careful, the most interesting. Some two-syllable adjectives have more than one standard form: quieter or more quiet; cleverer or more clever; narrower or more narrow; simpler or more simple.
examples: The diagram is more useful than the list.
This is the most simple explanation.
sections.note: Choose a conventional form for the adjective; both listed alternatives are accepted in this course.

sections.title: Irregular forms and far
sections.text: Good → better → best and bad → worse → worst. Far has two standard families: farther/farthest and further/furthest. Both are standard for distance; further alone also means additional or broader.
examples: The revised poster is better than the first draft.
This is the farthest classroom from the hall.

sections.title: Common mistakes to avoid
sections.text: Do not make a double comparison or superlative: say easier, not more easier; say the fastest, not the most fastest. Use one formation pattern only.
examples: The second clue is easier than the first.
She chose the most interesting article.

sections.title: Than, the, good and well
sections.text: A comparative often uses than: cleaner than the old table. A superlative adjective before a noun normally needs the: the cleanest table, unless another determiner already does the job. Use good for a noun or thing; use well for how an action is done.

miniCheck.sentence: The poster is _____ than the first draft.
miniCheck.explanation: Large ends in -e, so add -r: larger than.

miniCheck.sentence: Of the three displays, Nia's is the _____.
miniCheck.explanation: Good is irregular: good → better → best.

miniCheck.sentence: This is the _____ corner in the library plan.
miniCheck.explanation: Use the superlative quietest. The most quiet is also a valid standard alternative, but it is not an option here.
